Inscribed Square

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Move the triangle and the point P to make a square whose four corners all sit on the sides of the triangle.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or P, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Slide P along the base, then press "Show solution" to see where it belongs.
Look for the math

The old applet lets you grow a square inside a triangle and watch one corner hang free. A small change in where you start makes every square in the family change size together — and at just one place the free corner touches the third side.

A square with one corner free

Start with P on the base AB. The applet draws the perpendicular at P until it meets the line AC at p, and takes d = |Pp| as the side of a square. Its base runs from P to q along AB, its top edge ends at r, and p is on AC. Three corners touch the triangle; r is the dangling one. The logic test checks thousands of positions: the four sides stay equal and meet at right angles, and p stays on AC.

Where the free corner belongs

The page tells you to draw a line from A through the free corner r. Where that line meets BC is the corner of the square that really fits. This port draws that ray and the whole target square as a dashed green guide; the Java applet only drew the ray. If the base has length a and the triangle's height above it is h, the fitted square has side

s = a × h / (a + h)

The test confirmed this over a grid of triangles, including ones whose top corner is off to the side or below the base. The number does not depend on how far along AB the top corner sits. The applet's three little eyes open when r comes within one pixel of BC; the test checks that exact one-pixel boundary.

Scaling, not central symmetry

The original page says these squares come from one another by "central symmetry with center at A". That wording is a slip: a central symmetry keeps lengths, while squares started at two different points P have different sides. The true relation is a homothety centered at A: scaling by d2 / d1 sends the first trial square to the second, and the same scaling sends it to the fitted square. The logic test checks both statements and confirms the page's wording is wrong.

One solution or two?

The page adds that homothety gives an entirely different solution and that "in general the problem has two solutions". That is right for the three sidelines treated as whole lines: solving the two line equations gives two positive sizes, a×h/(a+h) and a×h/|a−h|. When a = h the second size is infinite, so only one square remains. Often the second square uses the extensions of the sides rather than the segments. The test counts the solutions over a grid and confirms both cases. The live cut-the-knot page now shows a GeoGebra construction; an archived 2006 capture is the one that still embeds this Java applet under the same address.

Try dragging C until the triangle is very tall, then press "Show solution" and compare the green square with the purple one.
